title: A Hymn for the Room
premise: Beatrix Pemberton, a late-night radio host in the dying village of Hollowmere, has spent a decade fielding calls from listeners who turn out to have died the week before — and telling themselves it's grief, hoaxes, or signal bleed. When the church bell that was melted down in 1911 rings across the village, Beatrix is pulled into the vestry where the parish's founding families once made a bargain: every hundred years, they invite something in to take their sins, and the village survives by feeding it one willing soul. Tonight the debt has come due, the descendants are locked inside with what they summoned, and Beatrix — whose dead callers were all previous offerings, still broadcasting from wherever it keeps them — must decide whether to expose the bargain, break it, or pay it. The story ends at sunrise: Beatrix takes the microphone one last time, gives the thing a voice instead of a body, and lets the whole county hear what Hollowmere did, dissolving the bargain but not escaping its price.
about_author: Noor Kavanagh is the pen name of a former community-radio producer who spent three years archiving dead-air recordings from rural stations before turning to fiction. They write horror about small places, old debts, and the voices that refuse to stop transmitting.

chapters.title: Dead Air
chapters.summary: Beatrix hosts 'The Night Line' from a cramped studio above the Hollowmere post office, taking a call from a woman who describes her own funeral from last Tuesday. Beatrix logs it as another hoax, but her hands shake. POV: Beatrix. Emotional beat: the practiced calm of someone who has explained away too much for too long.

chapters.title: The Bell That Isn't
chapters.summary: Walking home past the roofless church, Beatrix hears a single deep bell toll — though St. Aldric's bell was melted for scrap in 1911. Old-timer Wilf Corrie crosses himself and tells them the bell only rings when the parish owes. POV: Beatrix. Emotional beat: dread arriving on schedule, like weather.

chapters.title: Listeners
chapters.summary: Beatrix digs through ten years of call archives and finds every impossible caller died within days of phoning — always in October, always in multiples of seven. A new call comes in mid-search: their own voice, asking for help. POV: Beatrix. Emotional beat: the collapse of a decade of rationalizations.

chapters.title: The Founding Families
chapters.summary: In the county records office, Beatrix learns of the seven families who endowed St. Aldric's in 1811 and the 'Harvest Covenant' struck out of every ledger. Six surnames still live in Hollowmere. The seventh line ended in 1911 — the year the bell was melted. POV: Beatrix. Emotional beat: history snapping into focus like a trap closing.

chapters.title: Vespers
chapters.summary: The six descendants receive identical letters summoning them to the vestry at dusk. Beatrix, tipped off by a dead caller's warning, follows them in. The door seals behind the last arrival; the melted bell hangs impossibly in the dark, ringing without sound. POV: Beatrix. Emotional beat: the moment the explanation runs out.

chapters.title: What Was Invited
chapters.summary: Trapped in the vestry, the group finds the covenant written in a psalter's margins: feed it one willing soul each century, and it takes nothing else. It has been waiting since midnight. It is patient, courteous, and everywhere in the room's shadows. POV: Beatrix. Emotional beat: terror wearing the mask of politeness.

chapters.title: The Descendants
chapters.summary: Character chapter: farmer Ada Thorne denies everything; solicitor Marcus Hale lawyers at the dark; teenage twins Ivy and Rowan Fenn bicker to keep fear at bay; Dr. Priya Nair checks pulses that aren't there; elderly Ezra Mowbray simply says he's known since he was nine. POV: rotating close thirds. Emotional beat: six strangers discovering they were born into a debt.

chapters.title: First Offering
chapters.summary: The thing asks, gently, for a volunteer. Marcus volunteers immediately — then recants when it shows him what willingness actually costs. It takes a lock of his hair as 'earnest money,' and his reflection stops moving. POV: Marcus. Emotional beat: courage revealed as performance.

chapters.title: Signal Through the Wall
chapters.summary: Beatrix's phone picks up the studio frequency from inside the sealed vestry. Through static, the dead callers coach them: it cannot take an unwilling soul, but it can wait, starve, and wear you down until willingness seems like mercy. Sunrise is eleven hours away. POV: Beatrix. Emotional beat: grim hope with a countdown attached.

chapters.title: The 1911 Account
chapters.summary: Ezra recounts what his grandmother saw: the last offering was a girl who refused at the final moment, so the parish melted the bell to sever the covenant halfway — leaving the thing half-invited ever since. Every death since, every strange call, has been leakage. POV: Ezra. Emotional beat: inherited guilt becoming comprehensible.

chapters.title: Hunger
chapters.summary: Hours four through six. The vestry grows colder; food rots instantly; the twins' phone batteries die at 3:33 again and again. The thing begins speaking in their own voices, making kind offers — rest, warmth, an end to fear. Ivy starts listening. POV: Ivy. Emotional beat: exhaustion weaponized.

chapters.title: Ada's Bargain
chapters.summary: Ada tries to renegotiate alone: her life for the others' release. The thing agrees too easily, and Beatrix realizes via the dead callers that a solo deal would bind the whole village tighter than before. She talks Ada down seconds before consent. POV: Ada, then Beatrix. Emotional beat: sacrifice curdling into manipulation.

chapters.title: The Bell Speaks
chapters.summary: The melted bell finally sounds — audible now — and everyone hears the 1911 girl's voice inside it: she never stopped refusing, and her refusal is the only reason Hollowmere still exists. She begs them not to finish what their ancestors started. POV: Beatrix. Emotional beat: awe and grief entwined.

chapters.title: Rowan Runs
chapters.summary: Panic breaks the group: Rowan smashes a window and flees into the churchyard. Outside, the night folds around him; he returns changed, walking backward, smiling wrong, insisting the exit is lovely. The thing demonstrates it can hold souls even without consent — if they come to it. POV: Rowan. Emotional beat: the rules just got worse.

chapters.title: Priya's Diagnosis
chapters.summary: Priya, methodical even now, maps the thing's behavior: it strengthens near spoken consent, weakens near recorded truth. She realizes Beatrix's radio rig isn't incidental — broadcast is testimony, and testimony is the one thing it can't digest. POV: Priya. Emotional beat: science as a candle in a huge dark.

chapters.title: The Eighth Caller
chapters.summary: A call comes through no one dialed: the 1911 girl herself, Edith Mowbray — Ezra's great-aunt. She explains the loophole: the covenant requires a soul given willingly AND witnessed by the parish. If the giving is witnessed by everyone, forever, the terms poison themselves. POV: Beatrix. Emotional beat: the plan assembling out of grief.

chapters.title: Hour Ten
chapters.summary: The thing drops courtesy. Shadows thicken; Marcus's missing reflection walks the walls; Ivy is found mid-prayer, consenting in whispers, and Beatrix physically drags her back. One hour to sunrise. Someone will break. POV: Beatrix. Emotional beat: white-knuckle endurance.

chapters.title: Willingness
chapters.summary: Ezra, ninety-one and tired, stands up: he'll go willingly, gladly, to buy the children time — and means it. The thing accepts, and begins to take him. Beatrix makes her choice: she grabs the studio transmitter cable snaking through the wall and goes live from inside the vestry. POV: Ezra, then Beatrix. Emotional beat: love and defiance in the same breath.

chapters.title: On Air
chapters.summary: Climax. Beatrix broadcasts the whole truth — names, dates, the covenant, Edith's century of refusal — to every speaker in Hollowmere and beyond. The parish itself becomes the witness. The thing, forced to be seen by all, chokes on the testimony; Ezra's soul slips free of its grip; the bell cracks down the middle. POV: Beatrix. Emotional beat: the price of survival paid in exposure, not blood.

chapters.title: Sunrise
chapters.summary: Dawn enters through the broken window. The vestry is ordinary again except for the split bell and Ezra, alive but hollowed, remembering nothing after age nine. The survivors walk out into a village that heard everything and pretends it didn't. POV: Beatrix. Emotional beat: survival that feels like both victory and theft.

chapters.title: The Last Broadcast
chapters.summary: Weeks later, Beatrix ends 'The Night Line' with a final episode reading the covenant aloud into the record, so no future generation can claim ignorance. The dead callers say goodbye one by one, Edith last, her voice finally at rest. The station sign-off plays over true silence. POV: Beatrix. Emotional beat: mourning as an act of justice.

chapters.title: Static
chapters.summary: Epilogue. Beatrix leaves Hollowmere, but in a motorway service station a radio left playing catches one word of static that sounds like thanks — or invitation. Somewhere, another village's bell is being weighed for scrap. Beatrix keeps driving. POV: Beatrix. Emotional beat: the quiet horror that debts like these are never only local.
